o: At second i the faulty program grabs exactly i bits from whichever stick currently has MORE free memory — stick 1 wins ties — and it crashes at the first second when neither stick can afford i. Example 1: (2,2) gives stick 1 one bit (1,2), then stick 2 two bits (1,0), and at second 3 nobody can pay, so the answer is [3,1,0]. Example 2 drains for five more seconds before stick 1 fails to fund second 6, leaving [6,0,4]. Because the demand i grows quadratically while total memory shrinks linearly, i(i+1)/2 must exceed the initial total before a crash — at most about sqrt(2 * (m1 + m2)), roughly 10^5 iterations even for 32-bit sticks, so direct simulation is the intended solution.
k: Crash time is bounded by roughly sqrt(2 * (memory1 + memory2)): the triangle number i(i+1)/2 must outgrow the total free bits.
Allocation always feeds the larger stick (tie goes to stick 1), so the lead flips back and forth as sticks drain unevenly.
While one stick dominates it absorbs CONSECUTIVE allocations; draining such runs in bulk skips most loop iterations.

a.i: Advance a second counter; if neither stick holds at least i bits, return the counter and both remainders. Otherwise subtract i from the larger stick (stick 1 on ties) and move on. Terminates in O(sqrt(total)) steps by the triangle-number bound.
s: If memory1 < i and memory2 < i, crash has occurred: return [i, memory1, memory2].
Subtract i from the stick with more memory; on equal memory subtract from memory1.
a.t: O(sqrt(m1 + m2)) — the loop runs until the triangle number i(i+1)/2 exceeds the initial total memory

a.n: Approach 2: Run-Length Drain of the Dominant Stick
a.i: Exploit the observation that consecutive seconds usually hit the SAME stick: while one stick is still the leader (>= the other) and can afford second i, keep subtracting inside an inner loop instead of re-entering the outer one each second. When the leader drops behind, roles flip naturally. The crash check is identical to plain simulation, but the loop body executes far fewer times; the worst-case bound is unchanged because each subtraction consumes at least one bit.
s: If memory1 < i and memory2 < i, return [i, memory1, memory2].
If memory1 >= memory2, drain memory1 while it stays >= memory2 and >= i, incrementing i each step; otherwise drain memory2 under the mirrored condition.
a.t: O(sqrt(m1 + m2)) worst case — drained bits still bound the loop — but typically several times fewer iterations than second-by-second simulation

w: Simulate — and resist inventing a closed form, because crash time depends on the DISTRIBUTION of memory, not just its sum: (5, 1) crashes at second 3 even though the total of 6 would "afford" second 4 by triangle numbers. Pitfalls: resolving ties toward stick 2 instead of stick 1, checking affordability after incrementing i, and returning the leftover amounts in swapped order. Follow-ups: prove the O(sqrt) bound formally, or derive exact closed-form results for special starting configurations such as equal memories.
